newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's economy to show moderate '97 growth - group.
newsitem.headline: Canada's economy to show moderate '97 growth - group.

text.p: Canada's economy, boosted by low interest rates, is expected to post growth of 2.9 percent in 1997, a private research foundation said on Thursday.

In the winter 1997 issue of its Canadian Outlook, the Conference Board of Canada raised its previous outlook from the 2.7 percent growth it had forecast in the autumn, but warned that the positive effect of low borrowing costs will be undermined by "extremely" high household debt, lackluster job creation and continuing public sector spending cuts.
The Board forecast 1998 growth of 2.7 percent.

"Canadians remain concerned about high household debt, job security and income prospects," the Board's vice president and chief economist Jim Frank said in a statement released with the outlook. "With savings rates at record low levels and modest income growth, consumers just won't be able to increase their spending this year."

The Board said Canada's economy would continue to rely on export growth. It said a projected a C$4.3 billion upturn in rela nect exports would contribute about 0.7 percentage points to total economic growth in 1997.

The think tank said growth of less than 2.0 percent in domestic demand, together with an output gap of over 4.0 percent and continuing government cutbacks, are likely to prompt another 25-basis point easing in Canadian short-term interest rates by mid-1997.
A basis point is 1/100 of a percentage point.

A decline in the yield of Canadian three-month T-bills to 2.75 percent by mid-1997 against an anticipated slight increase in U.S. short-term interest rates would widen spreads between Canadian and U.S. yields further to about 2.75 percentage points, the Board said.
"The lower Canadian rates, together with previous declines, will regenerate a stalled housing recovery while easing the financial burden on debt-laden households," the Conference Board said.
The group forecast stable Canadian interest rates for the second half of 1997 and into 1998.
It said strong fundamentals, especially Canada's improving fiscal positions and current account balance, would contribute to an increase in the value of the Canadian dollar.
"Foreigners now accept that better fundamentals will produce a currency appreciation that compensates for the loss of interest rate returns," the Board said.
The Conference Board said the Canadian dollar would reach US$0.765 by the end of 1998. The dollar, which has rallied in recent days, traded at US$0.747 on Thursday morning.
But the group said consumer spending was likely to rise by a meager 1.8 percent in 1997, after an estimated 2.1 percent increase in 1996.
"The root cause of the weak consumer outlook is poor income prospects," the group said.

Canadians' real disposable income was forecast to rise only 1.0 percent in 1997 after remaining virtually unchanged in 1996. The personal debt-to-income ratio was at a record 95.1 percent, while the personal savings rate was at a 25-year low of 5.1 percent.
Nevertheless, the Conference Board said low interest rates were likely to spur a 9.9 percent increase in real residential construction in 1997 and 6.4 percent in 1998.
Investment in real machinery and equipment would remain strong, rising 8.5 percent in 1997 and 9.0 percent in 1998, after a 8.3 percent increase in 1996, the Board said.
